newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sentences British spy to 10 years.
newsitem.headline: Russia sentences British spy to 10 years.

text.p: Russia's top court sentenced a former Russian company manager to 10 years' hard labour and confiscated his property on Wednesday for spying for Britain.

A court official said Vadim Sintsov, who was arrested in January 1994, pleaded guilty at the trial, which was conducted by the military bench of the Supreme Court. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed.
The official said Sintsov, 62, had been given much less than the maximum 20 years for "cooperating with the court".
The British embassy in Moscow said it had no comment on the case.

The trial was held behind closed doors and court officials did not elaborate on what secrets were divulged by Sintsov, a one-time director in charge of foreign relations at a high-technology military industrial plant.

Russian newspapers have said Sintsov was recruited while on a trip to Britain in 1993 and that he had disclosed details of Russian arms supplies to the Middle East to Britain's Secret Intelligence Service, also known as MI6.

Grey-haired and bespectacled, Sintsov appeared on NTV commercial television in March, three months after he had been arrested. He said he had worked for British intelligence for only one year and had been paid $12,000.
Sintsov's trial coincided with a series of statements by Russian security officials saying foreign spy services were stepping up their operations in Russia.
Senior officials from the FSB federal security service have said that in 1996 alone they uncovered 27 professional foreign spies and 60 Russian citizens working for foreign intelligence services.
A former Russian Foreign Ministry worker, Platon Obukhov, arrested last year on charges of spying for the British is still awaiting trial.
Obukhov's family says the young man, who held a technical position in a crucial ministry department, was mentally unstable and should be treated by doctors rather then prosecuted.

Last month, FSB chief Nikolai Kovalyov called on foreign spies and their Russian operatives to call a hotline and become double agents. Kovalyov said last week the hotline had been a success and added, tantalisingly, that people would be surprised when he gave details.
